analysis.one_liner: Bans sellers from charging unconscionably excessive prices in federally declared disaster areas.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would make disaster-area price gouging a federal offense, never left committee and died without a single cosponsor or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the President declares a major disaster, this bill would make it unlawful for 180 days to sell essentials like food, water, fuel, building supplies, or rental housing at prices that are unconscionably excessive and take unfair advantage of the disaster. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the ban, on top of existing state price-gouging laws, which the bill would not override. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: People in disaster zones — hurricane and wildfire victims who suddenly need water, generators, fuel, lodging, and repairs — would be protected from sellers dramatically raising prices during the emergency. State attorneys general would gain a federal tool to sue gougers and win restitution for residents.

how_it_helps.text: For 180 days after a major disaster declaration, selling consumer goods or services in the affected area at an unconscionably excessive price that takes unfair advantage of the disaster would be unlawful [S3].
Covered items include food, water, ice, fuel, building supplies, repair and debris-removal services, residential construction, and housing or storage rented to consumers [S3].

The FTC would enforce the ban under its unfair-or-deceptive-practices authority, and state attorneys general could sue in federal or state court for injunctions, civil penalties, and restitution for state residents [S3].
The bill does not preempt or limit any stronger state or local anti-gouging law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers in disaster areas — retailers, hotels and landlords, contractors, and fuel and supply distributors — would give up the ability to raise prices steeply during emergencies, and could face FTC penalties or state lawsuits if they did.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sellers of goods and housing in disaster zones

drawbacks.text: The standard allows price increases that reasonably reflect higher supply costs, added risk, or forgone sales, but critics of anti-gouging laws generally argue that capping prices during shortages can discourage outside suppliers from rushing goods into a damaged area, leaving shelves emptier than higher prices would [S3].

The core standard — 'unconscionably excessive' — is a judgment call assessed case by case against prior prices and comparable sellers, which creates uncertainty for businesses and discretion for enforcers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but narrow: it lasts only 180 days, applies only in federally declared disaster areas, and lets sellers pass along genuinely higher costs. The main cost is a modest risk that price caps slightly slow emergency resupply, and the bill's overlap with existing state gouging laws means its practical addition would have been federal enforcement muscle. On balance a targeted consumer protection with limited downside.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee the week it was introduced, and no one on the committee ever moved it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on October 31, 2017, during a fall of major hurricanes and wildfires [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; on November 3 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection [S5].
No further action was ever taken, and the bill attracted zero cosponsors [S4][S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill expired without ever leaving committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of essentials in disaster zones — retailers, hotels, landlords, contractors, and fuel distributors — kept the ability to raise prices steeply after disasters without facing federal penalties, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sellers of essentials in disaster zones

sides.party_line_note: A House Democrat introduced the bill with no cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Retailers and distributors of emergency essentials (grocers, fuel, generators, building supplies)
industries.note: These sellers could no longer charge steeply elevated prices for water, fuel, and supplies during a disaster without risking FTC penalties or state lawsuits. Their gain from scarcity pricing comes directly out of disaster victims' pockets.

industries.industry: Hotels, landlords, and short-term rental operators
industries.note: Rental housing and storage in disaster areas would fall under the price cap, limiting surge pricing for displaced families seeking lodging. This is exactly the market where gouging complaints after hurricanes have been most common.
Residential construction, reconstruction, repair, and debris removal are covered services, so post-disaster pricing would have to stay tied to prior norms and actual added costs.
